newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FMC's Argentine mine said going well.
newsitem.headline: FMC's Argentine mine said going well.

text.p: Startup at FMC Corp's Fenix lithium project in Argentina is progressing well despite minor hitches and small cost overruns, and significant lithium output should begin this year, a firm official said.

"As far as the schedule goes, we're probably a couple of days behind schedule. There are no particular problems of any sort," Fenix project manager Richard Troell told Reuters by telephone from the site.
He said that the mine had started limited work with brine but that the first lithium compound production would begin "some time later this year."

The Fenix mine is being built at 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level around a salt lake straddling the northwestern provinces of Catamarca and Salta. Troell said that inconveniences caused by the awkward location, such as some difficulty finding skilled labor, had caused small delays and slightly pushed up costs.

"In an overall sense it has increased costs slightly, but not astronomically," Troell said, "From an overall expense viewpoint it has not been that much different from what was envisioned at the beginning."

The $68-million project is based on solution mining the Salar del Hombre Muerto, which means "Dead Man's Saltlake" in Spanish. But it will also exploit the smaller Pocitos saltlake. Output will be pumped to a chemical production site at General Guemes, about 100 miles (160 km) away.
Argentina's young winter has struck hard so far this year, and the minesite was recently isolated for three days by a heavy snowfall, Troell said.
"It was just a headache. We had the food, the fuel, we had most of the materials, so it was just business as usual," Troell said, "But it was extremely cold."
He added that the isolation did not prevent the mine crew celebrating a million man hours worked without lost time or recordable injury.
"We have had over two million man hours without a serious injury, and no fatalities," Troell said.
The mine workforce is now about 100, but was more than 600 when construction work -- contracted out to Argentine firm Techint -- was it its height.

"When you roll in all the logistics of the location and the climate, and you compare it to a job in Buenos Aires, then yes, there have been a lot of hitches, but when you take everything into account, then in my opinion the project has gone really smootlhy," Troell said.
To produce 45 million pounds, lithium carbonate equivalent, a year, Fenix will provide the first major lithium production in the world outside Chile or the United States.
It will enter a long cozy lithium market frazzled by the aggressive marketing of Chilean newcomers Sociedad Quimica y Minera de Chile, which started production at its Minsal mine last October.

The largest consumers of lithium carbonate, a fine white powder, are the glass, ceramics and aluminium industries. Demand is also strong from U.S. smelters where lithium is used for improving energy efficiency. It is also used, in smaller quantities, as a treatment for manic depression.
